issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires property while litigation concerning it is pending is bound by the final order in that litigation.
material_facts: The acquisition de-notification was challenged by the beneficiary society, and that challenge was pending before the Supreme Court when the petitioners purchased the land.
The Supreme Court later quashed the de-notification, thereby reviving the acquisition proceedings.
The petitioners argued that they were not bound because no interim order had prevented the purchase.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners were bound by the Supreme Court’s final order despite having purchased the land during the pending litigation and despite the absence of an interim order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the doctrine of lis pendens. A transferee pendente lite is bound by the decree as if a party to the litigation; a transfer cannot defeat the other party’s rights under the decree unless made with the court’s permission. The Court relied on K. Adivi Naidu v. E. Duruvasulu Naidu, Venkatrao Anantdeo Joshi v. Malatibai, Raj Kumar v. Sardari Lal, Sanjay Verma v. Manik Roy, Rajender Singh v. Santa Singh, and T.G. Ashok Kumar v. Govindammal.

rule.if: property_rights_litigation_pending and property_transferred_during_litigation and not transfer_with_court_permission and proceeding_to_apply_final_order

predicates.property_rights_litigation_pending: A proceeding concerning rights or interests in the property was pending.
predicates.property_transferred_during_litigation: A party transferred the property while that proceeding was pending.
predicates.transfer_with_court_permission: The transfer was made with the permission of the court hearing the proceeding.
predicates.proceeding_to_apply_final_order: A proceeding seeks to apply the final order made in the property litigation.
predicates.transferee_bound_by_final_order: The transferee is bound by the final order in the property litigation.

issues.definition: When property is transferred during pending property litigation without court permission, the transferee is bound by the final order when a proceeding seeks to apply it.

issues.legal_issue: A person who purchases land after public notice of its acquisition cannot challenge the acquisition proceedings on the basis of that purchase.
material_facts: The petitioners purchased the land after the preliminary acquisition notification had been issued.
The petitioners sought de-notification and challenged the refusal to give effect to the later de-notification order.
The Court held that the acquisition proceedings had revived after the earlier de-notification was quashed.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners could not challenge the acquisition proceedings; at most, they could claim compensation on the basis of their vendors’ title.
issues.legal_principle: A purchaser who acquires land after a notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does so at their own peril. The purchase does not bind the State or the acquisition beneficiary and confers no title against them, although the purchaser may claim compensation by stepping into the vendor’s shoes. The Court relied on V. Chandrasekaran v. The Administrative Officer and the authorities cited there, including Leela Ram v. Union of India, Smt. Sneh Prabha v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Meera Sahni v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi, and Tika Ram v. State of U.P.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity or continuation of a land acquisition.
predicates.purchase_after_public_acquisition_notice: The purchaser acquired the land after public notice that it was needed for acquisition.
predicates.purchaser_cannot_challenge_acquisition: The purchaser cannot challenge the acquisition on the basis of the purchase.

issues.definition: A purchaser who acquires land after public notice of its acquisition cannot use that purchase to challenge the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: Land that has vested in the State after possession is taken under an acquisition cannot be released from that acquisition.
material_facts: Possession of the land had been taken before the Minister ordered its de-notification.
The petitioners sought release of land after possession had been taken.
The Court found that possession had been taken under the acquisition and that the land had vested in the State free from encumbrances.
issues.conclusion: The land could not be released from acquisition after possession had been taken and it had vested in the State; the later de-notification order could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 16 or 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, taking possession vests the land in the State free from all encumbrances. Once vesting has occurred, the land cannot be divested and an application for release from acquisition is not maintainable. The Court relied on Lt. Governor of H.P. v. Sri Avinash Sharma, Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., Mandir Shree Sitaramji v. Land Acquisition Collector, and Smt. Sulochana Chandrakant Galande v. Pune Municipal Transport.

predicates.release_request_in_land_acquisition: A party requested that land be released from an acquisition.
predicates.possession_taken_under_acquisition: Possession of the land was taken under the acquisition.
predicates.land_vested_free_of_encumbrances: The land vested in the State free from encumbrances after possession was taken.
predicates.release_from_acquisition_unavailable: The land cannot be released from the acquisition.

issues.definition: A request to release acquired land cannot succeed when possession has been taken and the land has vested free from encumbrances.

issues.legal_issue: An earlier decision quashing a withdrawal from acquisition on both procedural and substantive grounds cannot be treated as having rested only on a procedural defect.
material_facts: The petitioners argued that the earlier Supreme Court decision quashed the withdrawal from acquisition only because the beneficiary society had not been heard.
The earlier decision stated that the withdrawal was also vitiated because its reason was wrong and that the acquisition had been properly initiated.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision had rejected the withdrawal on both the failure to hear the beneficiary and the lack of justification for withdrawal; it was not based only on a technical ground.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the terms of its earlier decision in State Govt. Houseless Harijan Employees Association v. State of Karnataka, which held that the withdrawal under Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was vitiated both because the beneficiary was not heard and because the reason for withdrawal was wrong.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_later_action_after: A proceeding challenges later action concerning an acquisition that was addressed in an earlier ruling.
predicates.earlier_ruling_found_withdrawal_unjustif: The earlier ruling found that the withdrawal from acquisition lacked substantive justification.
predicates.party_claims_earlier_ruling_was_only_pro: A party argues that the earlier ruling rested only on a procedural defect.
predicates.earlier_ruling_rejected_withdrawal_on_pr: The earlier ruling rejected the withdrawal for both procedural and substantive reasons.

issues.definition: When an earlier ruling found a withdrawal substantively unjustified as well as procedurally defective, it cannot be treated as having rejected the withdrawal only for procedural reasons.
